body.text: In brief
• Since Israel's election, a new parliament has been sworn in, and a Gadi Eisenkot ally has been elected speaker.
• The battle to form government is ongoing, with Eisenkot now facing three main options to secure power.
It's been nearly four weeks since Israel's election, but the country still doesn't know who its leader is.

A new parliament has been sworn in, and Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival in the inconclusive October vote, has been tasked with forming the next government. He has until next month to do so.

But his 48-seat bloc is well short of the 61 needed for a majority in the Israeli parliament, known as the Knesset. Parties in Netanyahu's coalition won 53 seats, while two Arab parties secured a historic 19 seats.
As is typical in Israeli politics, Eisenkot's camp — a loose alliance of parties across the ideological spectrum — must therefore secure support from other parties to govern.
However, its members remain divided over who to join forces with.

His options include forming a minority government with support from Arab parties on key votes, building a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties from Netanyahu's bloc, or forming a unity government with Netanyahu — an outcome the prime minister has been pushing for.
Meanwhile, Netanyahu has sought to cast doubt on the election results, claiming the surge in support for Arab parties was the result of voter fraud.
Election officials have said they are investigating potential misconduct but they have seen no evidence of fraud that could have influenced the vote's outcome.

Middle East analyst Ran Porat, a researcher at Monash University's Australian Centre for Jewish Civilisation, told SBS News he's watched Israeli politics for years and views the current situation as one of the "most challenging times" in Netanyahu's long political career.
"I don't see, as of now, a path forward for him to stay in office," he said..
So, what's happened since the election, and what comes next?
Eisenkot gets first chance to form government
On 8 November, Israeli President Isaac Herzog granted Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a new government.
Though Eisenkot's camp won fewer seats than Netanyahu's, he secured more endorsements from Knesset members after two Arab-led parties, which strongly oppose Netanyahu, backed his bid.
He has 28 days to assemble a government. If he fails, Herzog can grant a 14-day extension before offering another lawmaker the opportunity to try.
In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, Eisenkot said negotiations were continuing on several fronts, including with ultra-Orthodox parties and Netanyahu's Likud.

He said he would try to put forward a national emergency government if efforts to form a broader coalition failed, signalling he could consider a minority government with external support from Arab parties.
According to Porat, efforts are focused on reaching an agreement with ultra-Orthodox parties, while talks with Likud are unlikely to produce a unity government.
New Knesset sworn in
Israel's newly elected parliament was sworn in on 10 November, with Netanyahu remaining caretaker prime minister while efforts to form a government continued.

With support from the Arab parties, the newly sworn-in parliament could still deliver on some of Eisenkot's campaign promises, such as potentially setting up a commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks, something backed by the Arab parties but largely opposed by Netanyahu.
At the swearing-in ceremony, Herzog told Knesset members: "You must do everything to avoid a repeat election".
Eisenkot ally elected as speaker of the Knesset
On 17 November, Israel's parliament elected a new speaker, marking a potential first step in rolling back Netanyahu's agenda.
Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot's Yashar party, was elected with 66 votes. He replaced Amir Ohana, a politician from Netanayhu's Likud.
The speakership is a powerful position that wields considerable influence, including over what legislation is brought to a vote.

Kahana will have the ability to advance bills prioritised by the Eisenkot-led bloc, including proposals to establish an October 7 inquiry, impose term limits on the prime minister and repeal laws passed by the previous Netanyahu-led government that critics said curtailed the judiciary's powers.
Porat likened the potential reversal of Netanyahu's policies to US President Donald Trump's efforts to undo his predecessor Joe Biden's agenda.
"Think of it as like when Trump went into office; his first mission was to un-Biden everything," Porat said.
"So now, in this interim period until there is a government — and it's going to take a few weeks — the speaker can move forward lots of bills that are undoing the Netanyahu government."
What happens next?
Despite the progress made in parliament, Eisenkot still faces significant obstacles to forming government.
Avigdor Lieberman, a nationalist party leader in his bloc, has ruled out supporting a minority government reliant on Arab parties.
Meanwhile, negotiations with ultra-Orthodox parties face a major sticking point: military conscription.
Ultra-Orthodox parties want to preserve exemptions from compulsory service for members of their communities, while Eisenkot campaigned to expand military service.

Netanyahu has been calling for a unity government with Eisenkot, arguing it would address security challenges and could "eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all". He has warned against any attempts to form a minority government, saying it would be "weak and dangerous".
Eisenkot has accused him of playing tricks and sowing division.
Porat believes a government will be formed in the coming weeks.
"The best chance, as of now, is a government between Eisenkot's bloc and the ultra-Orthodox," he said.
If Eisenkot fails to form government next month, another candidate, potentially Netanyahu, could be tasked with trying to assemble a government.

Should that effort also fail, Knesset members would have a further 21 days to nominate a candidate who can secure a parliamentary majority. If no government can be formed, Israel would face another election.
— With additional reporting by Reuters and Agence-France-Presse
